![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14269128/assets/fa1f79a764667a0da3f5464a2a594eec94c14bbe748518758194ee69879900e9.png)

A child $C$ is flying a balloon $B$ with a $120\,\text{cm}$ length of string. If the balloon is rising vertically at a constant speed of $2\,\text{cm/s},$ at what rate is the angle of elevation $\theta $ increasing when $\theta ={45}^{∘}?$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14269128/assets/3ca3fa1fe2759b972b9056c8a0b6c0f9a50058517a169e24c9a1999005719b2d.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the balloon's height, and $z$ is the distance between the child and the balloon. The quantity $z=120$ centimeters does not change with time because the string's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{120} \\ y & =120\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(120\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(120\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Converting the given information from degrees to radians, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2$ and $\theta ={45}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\pi }{{180}^{∘}}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(120\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{1}{60} & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{60}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{60}$ radians per second.
